3146300.Title: A cluster of Pallister-Hall syndrome cases, (congenital hypothalamic hamartoblastoma syndrome)

abstract.1: We report on three infants with hand anomalies and congenital hypopituitarism.
abstract.2: In two of the cases, a hypothalamic tumor was found; the third infant died without postmortem brain studies.
abstract.3: Family history in the first case suggested possible familial recurrence; the mother's sister had died at 17 hr of age with polydactyly, microglossia, and flat nasal bridge (no autopsy done).
abstract.4: Our second case was born by cesarean section after a pregnancy complicated by extremely low maternal estriols.
abstract.5: At birth, hypopituitarism was diagnosed, a cranial CT scan was read as normal, and hormonal replacement was begun with thyroxine, hydrocortisone, and growth hormone.
abstract.6: At 11.5 mo of age she developed seizures; and a repeat CT scan showed a mass extending beneath the hypothalamus.
abstract.7: This tumor was removed surgically at 12 mo, the first successful treatment of this disorder.
abstract.8: Our third possible case had a bifid epiglottis, hypopituitarism, and hand anomalies.
abstract.9: A CT scan at birth failed to reveal a mass in the hypothalamus.
abstract.10: This child died from complications of untreated hypopituitarism, and no neuropathology studies were done.
abstract.11: These three cases were conceived between March 10th and April 17th in three different years in three geographically contiguous counties of Vermont.
abstract.12: Clustering in time and space and possible familial recurrence, in one of these cases, suggest a possible gene/environment interaction.

adaptation2.1: We report on three infants born with hands born with hand defects and defects of the pituitary gland, which regulates body functions and growth through chemical substances called hormones.
adaptation2.2: Two of the newborns had hypothalamic tumors (noncancerous growths in the base of their brains). The brain of the third newborn was not examined.
adaptation2.3: In one case, the disease runs in the family. The mother's sister died at the age of 17. She had extra fingers, extremely small tongue, and flat nose.
adaptation2.4: The mother of the second newborn had very low levels of estriol, a hormone made during pregnancy that is used to measure the unborn baby's health.
adaptation2.5: When this baby was born, brain imaging was normal, but the levels of hormones that regulate growth and development were low. Treatment with growth and other hormones was started.
adaptation2.6: At 11.5 months the baby started having seizures. A new brain imaging showed a mass in the lower part of the brain.
adaptation2.7: Surgery to remove this mass at 12 months was the first successful treatment of this disorder.
adaptation2.8: The third newborn had a split in the flap that protects the windpipe, lack of hormones that regulate growth and development, and abnormal hands.
adaptation2.9: Brain imaging at birth did not show a mass in the lower part of the brain.
adaptation2.10: This child died from complications of a brain mass that was not showing in the image.
adaptation2.11: These three babies were conceived between March 10th and April 17th in three different years in three neighboring counties of Vermont.
adaptation2.12: Close locations and possible other PHS cases in one of these families suggest inheritance and environment might interact.

9054938.Title: GLI3 frameshift mutations cause autosomal dominant Pallister-Hall syndrome

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS, M146510) was first described in 1980 in six newborns.
abstract.2: It is a pleiotropic disorder of human development that comprises hypothalamic hamartoma, central polydactyly, and other malformations.
abstract.3: This disorder is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait and has been mapped to 7p13 (S. Kang et al.Autosomal dominant Pallister-Hall syndrome maps to 7p13. Am. J. Hum. Genet. 59, A81 (1996)), co-localizing the PHS locus and the GLI3 zinc finger transcription factor gene.
abstract.4: Large deletions or translocations resulting in haploinsufficiency of the GLI3 gene have been associated with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome (GCPS; M175700) although no mutations have been identified in GCPS patients with normal karyotypes.
abstract.5: Both PHS and GCPS have polysyndactyly, abnormal craniofacial features and are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, but they are clinically distinct.
abstract.6: The polydactyly of GCPS is commonly preaxial and that of PHS is typically central or postaxial.
abstract.7: No reported cases of GCPS have hypothalamic hamartoma and PHS does not cause hypertelorism or broadening of the nasal root or forehead.
abstract.8: The co-localization of the loci for PHS and GCPS led us to investigate GLI3 as a candidate gene for PHS.
abstract.9: Herein we report two PHS families with frameshift mutations in GLI3 that are 3' of the zinc finger-encoding domains, including one family with a de novo mutation.
abstract.10: These data implicate mutations in GLI3 as the cause of autosomal dominant PHS, and suggest that frameshift mutations of the GLI3 transcription factor gene can alter the development of multiple organ systems in vertebrates.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) was first described in 1980 in six newborns.
adaptation2.2: It is caused by a single gene that is involved in development of multiple body parts. The problems include a non-cancer mass in the lower part of the brain and extra fingers and toes, among others.
adaptation2.3: This disorder is passed down by either parent, and the involved gene is located on chromosome 7, associating PHS with the gene called GLI3.
adaptation2.4: Variants of the the GLI3 gene in which some genetic information is missing or misplaced are associated with Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome (GCPS) that affects development of the hands, feet, head, and face.
adaptation2.5: Patients with both PHS and GCPS have extra or merged fingers and toes, and abnormal heads and faces. Both PHS and GCPS are passed down from either parent, but the clinical signs of these diseases are different.
adaptation2.6: The additional finger in GCPS is usually located next to the thumb. In PHS, the extra finger is in the center or next to the little finger (pinky). The extra toes follow the same pattern: in GCPS the sixth toe is next to the big toe.
adaptation2.7: No reported cases of GCPS have non-cancer growth in the lower part of the brain, and PHS does not cause increased distance between the eyes or broadening of the nose or forehead.
adaptation2.8: Because the generic changes for PHS and GCPS share the location on the chromosome, we study GLI3 as a gene potentially responsible for PHS.
adaptation2.9: We describe two PHS families with large changes in the GLI3 gene. In one family the change is new and there is no family history of PHS.
adaptation2.10: The data show that changes in the GLI3 gene, which are passed down in the family or happen for the first time, cause PHS. Large-scale  changes in the GLI3 gene can change the development of  many tissues and organs.

15617553.Title: Psychiatric and neuropsychological characterization of Pallister-Hall syndrome

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare, single-gene, malformation syndrome that includes central polydactyly, hypothalamic hamartoma, bifid epiglottis, endocrine dysfunction, and other anomalies.
abstract.2: The syndrome has variable clinical manifestations and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
abstract.3: We sought to determine whether psychiatric disorders and/or neuropsychological impairment were characteristic of PHS.
abstract.4: We prospectively conducted systematic neuropsychiatric evaluations with 19 PHS subjects ranging in age from 7 to 75 years.
abstract.5: The evaluation included detailed clinical interviews, clinician-rated and self-report instruments, and a battery of neuropsychological tests.
abstract.6: Seven of 14 adult PHS subjects met diagnostic criteria for at least one DSM-IV Axis I disorder.
abstract.7: Three additional subjects demonstrated developmental delays and/or neuropsychological deficits on formal neuropsychological testing.
abstract.8: However, we found no characteristic psychiatric phenotype associated with PHS, and the frequency of each of the diagnoses observed in these subjects was not different from that expected in this size sample.
abstract.9: The overall frequency of psychiatric findings among all patients with PHS cannot be compared to point prevalence estimates of psychiatric disease in the general population because of biased ascertainment.
abstract.10: This limitation is inherent to the study of behavioral phenotypes in rare disorders.
abstract.11: The general issue of psychiatric evaluation of rare genetic syndromes is discussed in light of this negative result.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare disease caused by changes in a single gene (the basic unit of inheritance.) The abnormalities include extra fingers and toes, growth of non-cancer masses in the brain, changes in the flap that protect the windpipe, improper function of the endocrine system that regulates body functions through hormones, and other problems.
adaptation2.2: The signs of this disease vary and are passed down through either parent.
adaptation2.3: We studied if PHS causes any mental health problems.
adaptation2.4: We measured how well the brain is working in 19 PHS patients ranging in age from 7 to 75 years.
adaptation2.5: The evaluation included clinical examination, patients' reports and tests of brain functions.
adaptation2.6: Seven of 14 adults had at least one of the mental health conditions most commonly found in the public.
adaptation2.7: Three other patients had delays in mental development or low scores on the tests that measure how well the brain is working. The tests usually evaluate reading, use of language, attention, learning, reasoning, remembering, problem-solving, and more.
adaptation2.8: We did not find mental health problems specifically associated with PHS. The frequency of each of the problems in these patients was the same as expected in the group of 19 people.
adaptation2.9: The rate of mental problems in PHS cannot be compared to the overall rate of mental problems in the general population because of the way this study collected the data.

abstract.1: Clinical characteristics: Pallister-Hall syndrome (referred to as PHS in this entry) is characterized by a spectrum of anomalies ranging from polydactyly, asymptomatic bifid epiglottis, and hypothalamic hamartoma at the mild end to laryngotracheal cleft with neonatal lethality at the severe end.
abstract.2: Individuals with mild PHS may be incorrectly diagnosed as having isolated postaxial polydactyly type A.
abstract.3: Individuals with PHS can have pituitary insufficiency and may die as neonates from undiagnosed and untreated adrenal insufficiency.
abstract.4: Diagnosis/testing: The diagnosis of Pallister-Hall syndrome can be established in a proband with both hypothalamic hamartoma and mesoaxial polydactyly.
abstract.5: Identification of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in GLI3 confirms the diagnosis.
abstract.6: Management: Treatment of manifestations: Urgent treatment for endocrine abnormalities, especially cortisol deficiency; management of epiglottic abnormalities depending on the abnormality and the extent of respiratory compromise.
abstract.7: Bifid epiglottis, the most common abnormality, typically does not need treatment.
abstract.8: Standard treatment of anal atresia or stenosis; symptomatic treatment of seizures; elective repair of polydactyly; developmental intervention or special education for developmental delays.
abstract.9: Prevention of secondary complications: Biopsy or resection of hypothalamic hamartoma may result in complications and lifelong need for hormone replacement; seizures may begin or worsen with use of stimulants for attention deficit disorder.
abstract.10: Surveillance: During childhood, annual developmental assessment and annual medical evaluation to assess growth and monitor for signs of precocious puberty.
abstract.11: Genetic counseling: Pallister-Hall syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
abstract.12: Individuals with PHS may have an affected parent or may have the disorder as the result of a de novo pathogenic variant.
abstract.13: About 25% of individuals have a de novo pathogenic variant.
abstract.14: Persons with a de novo pathogenic variant are generally more severely affected than those with a family history of PHS.
abstract.15: The risk to offspring of an affected individual is 50%.
abstract.16: Prenatal testing for pregnancies at increased risk is possible if the pathogenic variant in the family is known.
abstract.17: The reliability of ultrasound examination for prenatal diagnosis is unknown.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) ranges from mild to severe cases. Mild cases include polydactyly, in which people have six fingers or toes,  a harmless split in the epiglottis (a small leaf-shaped structure that prevents food and drink from entering the windpipe) and hypothalamic hamartoma, a noncancerous growth in the base of the brain that can cause seizures and other problems. The severe cases include laryngotracheal cleft, a defect in which the baby's airway and food passages are connected, which can lead to newborn's death if the food and saliva get into the lungs.
adaptation2.2: Mild PHS might be confused with babies having one or more extra finger or toe at birth, called postaxial polydactyly type A.
adaptation2.3: In people with PHS pituitary gland, located in the brain, might not produce enough hormones (substances that regulate growth, metabolism and other functions). People with PHS may have adrenal insufficiency, a condition in which the adrenal glands do not produce enough hormones to control blood pressure, metabolism and the immune system. If these conditions are not recognized and treated in newborns, they may die.
adaptation2.4: Hypothalamic hamartoma (non-cancer growth in the brain) and extra fingers or toes may be caused by Pallister-Hall syndrome.
adaptation2.5: Genetic testing confirms the patients have PHS.
adaptation2.6: Urgent treatments are needed if the glands do not produce enough hormones, especially cortisol. The defect in the flap that covers the windpipe needs treatment if it can lead to problems with breathing.
adaptation2.7: Bifid epiglottis, the split in the flap that covers the windpipe, typically does not need treatment.
adaptation2.8: Standard treatments are used for problems with anus, such as narrowing of the anal canal. Patients can choose to repair extra fingers. Seizures are treated as needed. Special education and other support are provided for developmental delays.
adaptation2.9: Treatments of the problems caused by PHS can have complications. After surgery for the hypothalamic hamartoma patients may need to take hormones for the rest of their life. Drugs for attention deficit disorder may cause or worsen seizures.
adaptation2.10: Every year, children with PHS need evaluation of their mental development, growth, and signs of their body changing into that of an adult (puberty) too soon.
adaptation2.11: Either parent passes down the disease.
adaptation2.12: A child will have PHS if either parent passes down the disease or if a new variant develops before birth.
adaptation2.13: About a quarter of the PHS patients have a new harmful variant.
adaptation2.14: Persons with a new harmful variant have a more severe disease than those with a family history of PHS.
adaptation2.15: Chances of getting or not getting the disease from the parent  are equal.
adaptation2.16: If the harmful variant runs in the family, the developing baby may be tested during pregnancy.
adaptation2.17: It is not known if ultrasound during pregnancy will show PHS.

26604140.Title: Urogenital development in Pallister-Hall syndrome is disrupted in a cell-lineage-specific manner by constitutive expression of GLI3 repressor

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare disorder caused by mutations in GLI3 that produce a transcriptional repressor (GLI3R).
abstract.2: Individuals with PHS present with a variably penetrant variety of urogenital system malformations, including renal aplasia or hypoplasia, hydroureter, hydronephrosis or a common urogenital sinus.
abstract.3: The embryologic mechanisms controlled by GLI3R that result in these pathologic phenotypes are undefined.
abstract.4: We demonstrate that germline expression of GLI3R causes renal hypoplasia, associated with decreased nephron number, and hydroureter and hydronephrosis, caused by blind-ending ureters.
abstract.5: Mice with obligate GLI3R expression also displayed duplication of the ureters that was caused by aberrant common nephric duct patterning and ureteric stalk outgrowth.
abstract.6: These developmental abnormalities are associated with suppressed Hedgehog signaling activity in the cloaca and adjacent vesicular mesenchyme.
abstract.7: Mice with conditional expression of GLI3R were utilized to identify lineage-specific effects of GLI3R.
abstract.8: In the ureteric bud, GLI3R expression decreased branching morphogenesis.
abstract.9: In Six2-positive nephrogenic progenitors, GLI3R decreased progenitor cell proliferation reducing the number of nephrogenic precursor structures.
abstract.10: Using mutant mice with Gli3R and Gli3 null alleles, we demonstrate that urogenital system patterning and development is controlled by the levels of GLI3R and not by an absence of full-length GLI3.
abstract.11: We conclude that the urogenital system phenotypes observed in PHS are caused by GLI3R-dependent perturbations in nephric duct patterning, renal branching morphogenesis and nephrogenic progenitor self-renewal.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare disorder caused by changes in the gene called GLI3.
adaptation2.2: Patients with PHS have a variety of problems with reproduction and urinary organs, including poor development of the kidneys, backup of urine in the duct between the kidney and the bladder, swelling of the kidneys, or a shared opening for the birth canal  and the urinary tract.
adaptation2.3: It is not known how the specific problems arise
adaptation2.4: We show that variations in the GLI3 gene cause poor development of the kidneys, and a closed end in the duct that runs between the kidney and the bladder, which causes swelling of the kidneys and the duct.
adaptation2.5: Mice with the same change in the GLI3 gene also had two ducts that connected a kidney to the bladder
adaptation2.6: The abnormal development is caused by the lack of information the embryonic cells (cells that forms when eggs are fertilized)  need for proper development.
adaptation2.10: Using mutant mice, we show that the development of the reproduction and urinary organs  is controlled by the variants in the GLI3 gene.
adaptation2.11: Different problems in PHS are caused by the different mistakes in the development of the urinary organs due to the information provided by the variants of the GLI3 gene.

26768579.Title: The early history of Pallister-Hall syndrome-Buried treasure of a sort

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome was initially recognized under fairly unique circumstances involving exhumation of the very first case.
abstract.2: The first two cases had dramatic and unusual features including a hypothalamic hamartoblastoma, imperforate anus, an unusual type of polydactyly with the extra digit being central, hypopituitarism with secondary hypoadrenalism, and lethality after birth (probably due to hypoadrenalism).
abstract.3: Within a short time frame, four additional cases were identified.
abstract.4: As the full spectrum and variability of anomalies was recognized, it became clear that it was not such a rare disorder.
abstract.5: Shortly after familial cases were recognized, the responsible gene was identified at GLI3.
abstract.6: However, since other different conditions also involved GLI3, elaborating the domains of the gene and the types of mutations needed to be defined in order to have a clear correlation of the genotype-phenotype relations.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome was first identified in unearthed human remains.
adaptation2.2: The first two bodies had unusual features including a brain mass, missing anus, a sixth finger in the center, and death after birth.
adaptation2.4: As more cases were found, it became clear that PHS is not such a rare disorder.
adaptation2.5: Shortly after, it was recognized that the disease runs in the families due to changes in the gene called GLI3.
adaptation2.6: Other problems can be caused by changes in the same gene GLI3. Different changes in the different parts of the gene cause different problems.

abstract.1: Pallister Hall syndrome is autosomal dominant disorder usually diagnosed in infants and children.
abstract.2: Current diagnostic criteria include presence of hypothalamic hamartoma, post axial polydactyly and positive family history, but the disease has variable manifestations.
abstract.3: Herein we report Pallister Hall syndrome diagnosed in a family where both patients were adults.
abstract.4: A 59 year old man developed seizures 4 years prior to our evaluation of him, at which time imaging showed a hypothalamic hamartoma.
abstract.6: He did well until he had visual changes after a traumatic head injury.
abstract.7: Repeat MRI showed slight expansion of the mass with formal visual field testing demonstrating bitemporal hemianopsia.
abstract.8: There was no evidence of pituitary dysfunction except for large urine volume.
abstract.9: He underwent surgery to debulk the hamartoma and the visual field defects improved.
abstract.10: There was no hypopituitarism post-operatively, and the polydyspia resolved.
abstract.11: His 29 year old daughter also had seizures and hypothalamic hamartoma.
abstract.12: Both patients had had polydactyly with prior surgical correction in childhood.
abstract.13: The daughter underwent genetic testing, which revealed a previously undescribed heterozygous single base pair deletion in exon 13 of the GLI3 gene causing a frameshift mutation.
abstract.14: Further investigation into family history revealed multiple members in previous generations with polydactyly and/or seizures.
abstract.15: Pallister-Hall syndrome is caused by an inherited autosomal dominant or de novo mutation in GLI3 gene.
abstract.16: This rare syndrome has not had prevalence defined, however.
abstract.17: Generally, diagnoses are made in the pediatric population.
abstract.18: Our report adds to the few cases detected in adulthood.

adaptation2.1: Pallister Hall syndrome is passed down by one of the parents. It is usually diagnosed in infants and children.
adaptation2.2: It is diagnosed if it runs in the family, and the children have hypothalamic hamartoma (a non-cancer growth of tissues in the brain), and extra fingers or toes, but these are not the only signs of the disease.
adaptation2.3: We diagnosed Pallister Hall syndrome in a family where both patients were adults.
adaptation2.4: A 59 year old man developed seizures 4 years before we examined him. An imaging examination showed a hypothalamic hamartoma.
adaptation2.6: He did well until he had changes in eyesight after a head injury.
adaptation2.7: MRI showed the mass has expanded slightly and the patient's vision was missing in the outer half of both the right and left eye.
adaptation2.8: There were no signs of problems with the hormones made in the pituitary gland (which maintain body functions), except for large amount of urine.
adaptation2.9: The patient had surgery to reduce the hamartoma and his vision improved.
adaptation2.10: After the surgery, the pituitary gland functioned normally, and the patient no longer was excessively thirsty.
adaptation2.11: His 29 year old daughter also had seizures and hypothalamic hamartoma.
adaptation2.12: Both patients had surgery to remove the extra fingers in childhood.
adaptation2.13: The daughter had genetic testing that showed she had a variant that caused the disease.
adaptation2.14: Many family members in previous generations had extra fingers and seizures.
adaptation2.15: Pallister-Hall syndrome is caused by either parent passing down the disease or a new harmful change in the genes.
adaptation2.16: It is not known how many people have this rare disease.
adaptation2.17: Generally, the disease is recognized in children.
adaptation2.18: We described some of the few cases detected in adults.

abstract.1: Polydactyly is a relatively common abnormality in infants.
abstract.2: However, it can be a marker of a wide variety of neurological and systemic abnormality.
abstract.3: Hence, it is important for pediatrician and physician to have insight into the various association of this apparently innocuous anomaly.
abstract.4: In this write-up, we report an extremely rare syndrome associated with polydactyly that is Pallister-Hall syndrome.
abstract.5: A 10-month-old male child born by lower segment cesarean section presented with global delay associated with microcephaly, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, flat nose, short philtrum, incomplete cleft in the upper lip and hard palate, polydactyly, and syndactyly.
abstract.6: The child presented with repeated vomiting and crying episodes.
abstract.7: The patient was investigated which revealed a hypothalamic hamartomas.
abstract.8: Pallister-Hall syndrome is a very rare autosomal dominant genetic disorder due to mutation in GLI3 gene in the short arm of chromosome 7 with variable penetrance and expressivity.

adaptation2.1: Extra fingers or toes are relatively common in newborns.
adaptation2.2: It can be a sign of different problems with the nervous and other systems.
adaptation2.3: Doctors need to know about the conditions that cause extra fingers and toes.
adaptation2.4: Pallister-Hall syndrome is a rare condition associated with having extra fingers and toes.
adaptation2.5: A 10-month-old male child had a small head, unusually prominent forehead, increased distance between the eyes, flat nose, a shorter than normal distance between the upper lip and the nose, incomplete cleft (slit) in the upper lip and the roof of the mouth, extra fingers, and fused fingers.
adaptation2.6: The child vomited and cried repeatedly.
adaptation2.7: An examination showed the child had hypothalamic hamartomas, a non-cancer growth of tissue in the brain.
adaptation2.8: Pallister-Hall syndrome is a rare disorder passed down by one of the parents. It ranges from mild to severe.

abstract.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is an extremely rare syndrome of unknown prevalence with autosomal dominant inheritance due to GLI3 gene mutations classically characterized by the presence of a hypothalamic hamartoma and polydactyly.
abstract.2: Additional diagnostic criteria include bifid epiglottis, imperforate anus, small nails, hypopituitarism, growth hormone deficiency, and genital hypoplasia.
abstract.3: It is typically diagnosed in infancy and early childhood, presenting with seizures and/or precocious puberty due to the hypothalamic hamartoma, and with limb anomalies due to central polydactyly.
abstract.4: Our patient had presented with polysyndactyly at birth.
abstract.5: However, as this is not uncommon in infants and is usually as part of the sporadic, isolated form of polydactyly, no further work up was done.
abstract.6: He then presented at age 16 years with a headache and subjective visual changes, with brain imaging revealing a hypothalamic hamartoma.
abstract.7: He did not have a history of seizures or central precocious puberty.
abstract.8: Genotyping revealed a pathogenic variant affecting the GLI3 gene.
abstract.9: We encourage all clinicians to consider PHS or an associated syndrome with a clinical finding of polydactyly.
abstract.10: Further, as the natural history continues to reveal itself, this patient's presentation provides important new data to the broad phenotypic spectrum of PHS.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare disease. It is not known how many people have the disease. It is caused by harmful changes in the genes that are passed down by either parent. The disease is characterized by the presence of a hypothalamic hamartoma (a non-cancer growth in the brain) and extra fingers or toes.
adaptation2.2: Other signs include a split in the flap that protects the windpipe, missing or blocked opening to the anus, small nails, reduced function of the pituitary gland, which controls body functions and growth through chemical substances called hormones, dwarfism, and poor development of the reproductive organs.
adaptation2.3: It is usually recognized in infancy and early childhood by the presence of seizures, signs of the child's body changing to that of an adult too soon, and extra fingers or toes.
adaptation2.4: Our patient had extra and fused fingers at birth.
adaptation2.5: Because extra fingers are common and may have different causes, no tests were done.
adaptation2.6: At the age of 16 he started having headaches and changes in vision. Brain imaging showed a hypothalamic hamartoma, a non-cancer growth in the brain tissues.
adaptation2.7: He did not have seizures or premature puberty.
adaptation2.9: Clinicians should think about PHS when they see extra fingers and toes.
adaptation2.10: The disease signs in this patient add new knowledge about PHS.

abstract.1: Introduction: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by polydactyly, bifid or shortened epiglottis, visceral anomalies, hypothalamic hamartoma often combined with hypopituitarism.
abstract.2: PHS is characterized by significant variability in the expression of clinical symptoms.
abstract.3: The clinical course ranges from mild with a good prognosis to severe and which can lead to death during the neonatal period.
abstract.4: Case report: Two-years-old girl with facial dysmorphia, skeletal malformations of hand and feet and growth hormone deficiency.
abstract.5: PHS was diagnosed on the basis of the presented symptoms and genetic tests.
abstract.6: Summary: Skeletal malformations, such as polydactyly or oligodactyly, are a markers which can be associated with endocrinological disorders.
abstract.7: Quick and correct diagnosis would help in planning treatment during childhood and giving family counseling, including prenatal advice regarding the next pregnancy of the child's mother.

adaptation2.1: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS) is a rare disease passed down from one of the parents. Its signs are six fingers and toes, shortened or split flap that protects the windpipe, problems with the organs in the chest and belly, non-cancer mass in the brain that often causes problems with pituitary gland, which regulates body functions and growth.

adaptation2.4: We describe a two-year-old girl with deformities of the face, hand and feet and dwarfism.
